questions.q: Identify the three distinct supporting figures explicitly mentioned or strongly implied in the poem "जूही की कली" (excluding the poet-speaker).
questions.a: The three supporting figures are: (1) the child (बच्चा/सीपी) who asks "फिरंगी फूल है क्या?", (2) the gardener (माली) implied by the line "माली ने कहा", and (3) the personified night (रात) described as wearing a "मोती का मुकुट". A wrong answer that lists only human characters (e.g., only the child) reveals the misconception that supporting characters must be human; personified natural elements are equally vital in this poem.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet includes the child’s question "फिरंगी फूल है क्या?" — what does this dialogue reveal about the bud and the poem’s perspective on innocence?
questions.a: The child’s question highlights the bud’s exotic, delicate otherness ("फिरंगी") and mirrors the poet’s own wonder; it frames the bud through innocent eyes that see mystery rather than botany. A wrong answer that treats the question as mere plot decoration misses how the child’s voice amplifies the theme of fragile beauty by contrasting adult knowledge with childlike awe.

questions.q: Apply the "character function" framework to the gardener (माली): using two pieces of textual evidence, show how the gardener’s implied presence establishes the bud’s cultivated vulnerability.
questions.a: Step 1: Locate the line "माली ने कहा" — this establishes a caretaker who monitors the bud. Step 2: Note the gardener’s protective stance implied by "साँझ को ढाँप दिया" (covered at dusk). Step 3: Infer that the bud is not wild but nurtured, making its eventual fall more poignant. A wrong answer that ignores the gardener’s protective act fails to see how human care intensifies the tragedy of natural transience.

questions.q: Analyze how the personified night (रात) and dawn (प्रभात) function as contrasting supporting characters — one protective, one revelatory — and what this duality suggests about the bud’s existence.
questions.a: Night "wears a crown of dew" (मोती का मुकुट) and "covers" the bud, acting as a gentle guardian; dawn "kisses" (चूमती) the bud, exposing it to light and inevitable wilting. Together they frame the bud’s brief life between shelter and exposure. A wrong answer that treats both as merely descriptive imagery misses their active, almost parental roles that structure the poem’s temporal arc.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The poet-speaker is the most important supporting character because he mediates all other figures." Defend or refute using evidence from the poem’s structure.
questions.a: Refute: the poet-speaker is the observer, not a supporting character; the poem’s power comes from the bud’s direct interactions with the child, gardener, night, and dawn. The speaker’s voice appears only in the final reflective stanza ("मैंने देखा"), making him a framing device. A wrong answer that elevates the speaker confuses narrative perspective with character function, a common error in lyric analysis.

questions.q: Create a two-stanza addition to the poem where a new supporting character — the wind (हवा) — interacts with the bud, maintaining the poem’s tone and symbolic pattern.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) use the same meter and imagery density (e.g., "हवा आई दबे पाँव / कली को झुलाया धीरे"), (2) show the wind as both gentle and destructive, (3) end with a line that echoes the theme of transience. A poor answer that makes the wind merely "blow hard" ignores the poem’s nuanced personification where every natural force has dual tenderness and inevitability.
